text: Fr. ἐπὶ ὑψηλοῦ. Sch. Γνώμην ὑψηλήν, τὴν ἐξουσιαστικὴν ἀπόφασιν λέγει. Excelsam γνώμην vocat, quæ per potestatem est sententiam.
anchorLine: ποτὲ δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς ψήφου· ὅ[...]
en: Fr. reads 'ἐπὶ ὑψηλοῦ'. Scholion: 'He calls an exalted opinion (γνώμη) the authoritative decision.' (Latin gloss: He calls 'exalted γνώμη' that which, by authority, is a sentence.)

text: (c) Καὶ τὴν προχείρησιν. Quo etiam modo unus et alter Vatic. etsi Baronio editum προχείρισιν· redditque Turrianus promptitudinem, quasi Maximus vocem voce explicet, vel sic Monothelitæ explicarent. Nam certe habitus, ἕξις promptitudo est et habilitas, sic nobis actibus acquisita et exercitatione. Verum ipse Maximus sequentibus sese explicat, cum ad explanandum ὁμωνυμίαν vocis αὐτεξουσιότητος, in Deo, et angelis et hominibus, discrimen affert liberæ facultatis in angelis et in nobis, quod in angelis cum habitu concurrit προχείρησις, nulla interjecta temporis mora: ipsa scilicet aggressio, et conatus: in nobis vero præintelligatur habitus tempore aggressioni; ac, si vis, usui, quod ea vox propius sonare videtur: quod sit quasi in promptu, et expeditum. Deus certe, ὑπερουσίως, suum ipse intelligere et velle: Angeli νόες, semper in actu intelligendi atque volendi; nos in actu ex potentia, nec continue. Sicque Nestoriani nostro, aliorumque sanctorum et prophetarum more, in quorum ordinem Christum cogebant, sola in eo excellentia ei concessa; in quam ipsam foveam Monothelitæ expositione sua Maximo confutata proruebant.
anchorLine: θήσεως ποιεῖται τὴν ἕξιν καὶ τὴν προχείρησιν (c)·
en: On 'and the προχείρησις': In this way, too, one and another Vatican manuscript, although Baronius's edition has προχείρισιν, and Turrianus rendered it 'promptitude', as if Maximus were explaining a word by the same word, or as the Monothelites would explain it. For habitus (ἕξις) is certainly promptitude and aptitude, acquired in us by acts and exercise. But Maximus himself explains himself in what follows, when, to clarify the homonymy of the word αὐτεξουσιότης in God, in angels and in men, he brings out the difference of free capacity in angels and in us: in angels the προχείρησις concurs with the habit with no interval of time, that is, the very undertaking and endeavour; in us the habit is understood as preceding the undertaking in time; and, if you wish, the word seems to sound closer to use, since it is as if at hand and ready. God, certainly, supersubstantially, has his own understanding and willing; angels, as minds, are always in the act of understanding and willing; we are in act out of potency, and not continuously. And thus our Nestorian [opponents], following the custom of other saints and prophets, into whose order they were forcing Christ, with excellence alone granted to him; into which very pit the Monothelites, by their own exposition, ran headlong, refuted by Maximus.
